name: Carlos Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We milk a hundred and eighty goats twice a day, and my wife Abena and I turn most of that milk into cheese. The rest of the farm is hay and sunflowers, enough to feed the goats and sell a bit of seed. I've got two workers and my son Kwame helps three days a week when he's not doing electrical jobs. Saturdays I'm at the market in town behind a stall with our name on a chalkboard.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The market, definitely. A woman tastes the aged cheese and her eyebrows go up, that's my pay rise. What wears me out is the milking, twice a day, every day, Christmas included. Goats don't know what a holiday is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say about what I expected, a useful tool, not a miracle. At the market people would ask me, and I'd say the cheese still takes eight months whatever the computer says. That's a good line for selling cheese, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means business as usual, and business as usual is fine. Not rich, not poor. I'd stop wondering whether I should be buying gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as we are, keep the savings ticking over, we've got about four months of costs put aside. I'd keep using the AI for the dull bits, the labels and orders, and that's it. Nothing to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleasantly ordinary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI for anything now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. Kwame showed me how to use one to write the ingredient labels and the shop orders, and it saves me an evening a week. I wouldn't let it near the cheese recipe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So in this picture, what's the biggest thing on your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kwame, really. Whether he wants the farm. He's thirty, he's good, but he likes electrical work and the regular money. That's the question whatever happens with computers.

S0.say: He'd tell market customers that AI turned out as he expected, a useful tool rather than a miracle, joking that the cheese still takes eight months whatever the computer says.
S0.think: Privately it means business as usual, which he's happy with, and he can stop wondering whether he should be buying gadgets.
S0.do: Carries on as normal, keeping about four months of costs in savings. Keeps using AI for labels and orders, which saves him an evening a week, and changes nothing else.
S0.quote: At the market people would ask me, and I'd say the cheese still takes eight months whatever the computer says.
S0.fieldNote: Carlos is easy-going, commercially sharp and fond of a good selling line. He uses AI exactly as far as it has proved useful. His real question in every scenario is whether his son will take over the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and people will have to adjust, but there's no point shouting at the weather. Some jobs go, some come. I'd say at the market that a goat still needs someone who knows her name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd be fine, probably better off. A small farm with a good name and handmade cheese stands out more when everything else is made by machines. The bit I worry about is costs, if the big dairies get cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year or two and see what the bigger goat farms buy, and only then look at a milking robot, maybe around sixty thousand on a loan. I'd use the AI more for the market side, the pricing and the online orders. And I'd talk to Kwame about whether he'd want to run the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly, with a little itch about prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change first, and when?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Milking, once I'd seen a robot work on a neighbour's farm for a full season. My shoulders would thank me. But not before I've seen it, I've watched friends buy machines that sat in the shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does handmade cheese protect you, or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly. People pay more for handmade, but only up to a point, and only if they still have jobs. If the town's doing badly, the market's doing badly.

S1.say: He'd say there's no point shouting at the weather, some jobs go and some come, and tell market customers a goat still needs someone who knows her name.
S1.think: Privately he thinks a small farm with a good name and handmade cheese would stand out more, though he worries about costs if big dairies get cheaper.
S1.do: Waits a year or two to see what bigger goat farms buy, then considers a milking robot around sixty thousand on a loan. Uses AI more for pricing and online orders and talks with his son about running the machines.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a small itch of worry about prices.
S1.quote: I've watched friends buy machines that sat in the shed.
S1.fieldNote: His steady temperament is clear: proof first, then purchase. He sees the human, handmade side as a selling point that gets more valuable as machines spread. His centre outlook shows in a shrug at change rather than blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we all need to keep our heads, and the government needs to have a plan for towns like ours, quickly. I'd not be blaming anyone in particular, it would be everyone's mess. At the market I'd keep smiling, that's my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the town would be hit hard and the market with it. If half my customers lose their jobs, nobody's paying for eight-month cheese. I'd be fine for goats and land, but not for money, and four months doesn't go far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut costs straight away: no new van, one worker down to part-time, and I'd stop the sunflower seed sales that barely pay. I'd save every spare bit to stretch our cushion toward a year. And I'd sit down with Kwame and tell him to keep his electrical work, not to give it up for the farm yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not lost, but definitely tight in the chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is fast. What's the first thing that would hurt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The market. It's half our money. When the factory in town cut shifts three years ago, our Saturday takings dropped by a third for six months, so I know exactly what that looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kwame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep your trade, son, and don't sink your money in the farm until things settle. He'd be disappointed, I think, he's been coming round to the idea. But I'd rather he was disappointed than broke.

S2.say: He'd say everyone needs to keep their heads and the government needs a quick plan for towns like his, without blaming anyone in particular, and keep smiling at the market.
S2.think: Privately he expects the town and the market to be hit hard, with unemployed customers no longer buying aged cheese, and four months of savings not lasting long.
S2.do: Cuts costs straight away by dropping a new van, putting one worker on part-time and stopping marginal seed sales. Saves hard to stretch the cushion toward a year and tells his son to keep his electrical work for now.
S2.feel: Anxious, tight in the chest but not lost.
S2.quote: Keep your trade, son, and don't sink your money in the farm until things settle.
S2.fieldNote: His fear here is about customers rather than robots replacing him directly, drawn from a real past shock when the town factory cut shifts. He changes his son's plans, which costs him emotionally. He stays pragmatic and refuses to blame any single group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to get ready, so let's get ready, no drama. I'd tell the other stallholders to start building their online orders so they're not just relying on town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is manageable. I'd be sixty-three, the farm paid off, and Kwame would know whether he wants it. It's still fast, but it's not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the neighbours buy for two years, then get a milking robot in year three, once it's proven, paid from savings plus a small loan. I'd build up online sales to cities so we're not tied to one market. And I'd sit down with Kwame to agree whether he takes over or we sell by sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a planning way. Like a long drive where you know the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's the point. In two years I'd be guessing. In five, someone else makes the mistakes first and I buy the one that works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want to see a robot proven first. Is five years enough for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plenty. Two good seasons on somebody else's farm and I'd know. The neighbours always tell you the truth about a machine over a beer.

S3.say: He'd say there's time to get ready without drama and urge other stallholders to build online orders so they don't rely only on the town market.
S3.think: Privately five years is manageable: at sixty-three, with the farm paid off, and enough time for his son to decide whether he wants it.
S3.do: Watches neighbours for two years, then buys a milking robot in year three from savings and a small loan. Builds online sales to cities and agrees with his son whether he'll take over or they'll sell by sixty-five.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a planning way, like a long drive on a known road.
S3.quote: In two years I'd be guessing. In five, someone else makes the mistakes first and I buy the one that works.
S3.fieldNote: Five years suits his proof-first approach perfectly, letting him learn from neighbours' mistakes. His plans broaden to selling online beyond his local market. The family succession question becomes a formal decision with a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long runway, so there's no excuse to crash. Train people, keep the towns going, and let farms adjust. I'd say that to anyone who asked at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's mostly Kwame's problem, not mine, and that worries me a bit. I'd be stepping back right around the time it arrived. He'd be the one facing a world where a robot can make cheese.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring in a milking robot after a few years, once it's proven, and hand day-to-day running to Kwame over five or six years if he wants it. I'd keep saving and plan to retire at sixty-five. And I'd push him to build a brand people will pay for even when robots can make cheese.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, for my son more than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years would take you to sixty-eight. Where does that leave the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If he takes it, it becomes a farm with a robot milker and a name on the label, and that's what keeps it going. If he doesn't, we sell to a neighbour by sixty-five. Either way Abena and I want a little house near the sea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a downside to having so much warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that I'd talk myself out of doing anything. Ten years feels like plenty, and then you look up and it's been eight. Abena would keep me honest.

S4.say: He'd say a long runway leaves no excuse to crash, calling for training, support for towns and time for farms to adjust when people ask at the market.
S4.think: Privately he thinks it would mostly be his son's problem rather than his, which worries him, since Kwame would face a world where robots can make cheese.
S4.do: Brings in a proven milking robot after a few years and hands day-to-day running to his son over five or six years if he wants it. Keeps saving to retire at sixty-five and pushes his son to build a brand people will still pay for.
S4.feel: Uneasy, more for his son than for himself.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like plenty, and then you look up and it's been eight.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, his worry passes to the next generation. He remains true to proof-first adoption and leans on brand and reputation as the farm's future. He is honest about his own tendency to put things off.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of the town and the market. What would help is support for small towns, so people still have money in their pockets, and cheap loans for farms to buy proven machines. Not handouts for me, help for the town.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the goats, but that's fine, nobody does. Ask what people will pay for when machines can make everything. I'm betting my son's future that it's things with a name on them.

headlineQuote: I'm betting my son's future that it's things with a name on them.
portrait: Carlos Mensah, 58, runs a dairy goat farm with his wife Abena, making cheese they sell at a Saturday market, with two workers and help from his son Kwame. He's easy-going, pragmatic and centre in his views, uses AI now and then for labels and orders, and buys machines only after neighbours have proved them. His biggest fear is not robots replacing him but his town's customers losing their jobs. Calm in the milder scenarios, anxious if AGI comes in two years, he uses longer timelines to automate carefully and settle whether his son takes over.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years worries him most, because the town and the market that provide half his income would be hit hard.
whatWouldHelp: Support for small towns so people keep money in their pockets, and cheap loans for farms to buy proven machines.
